recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each move in order.

steps.label: Reduce the last two angles
steps.margin_note: First mark. cos(5π/8) and cos(7π/8) both come out NEGATIVE, which turns two of the brackets from (1 + …) into (1 − …).
steps.memory_tip: Both reduce NEGATIVE, which turns two brackets from (1 + …) into (1 − …).
lines: The last two angles are π minus the first two:

recall.must_convey: That cos(5π/8) = −cos(3π/8) and cos(7π/8) = −cos(π/8), turning two brackets into differences.
accept: the last two cosines are negative so those brackets become one minus
cos five pi by eight is minus cos three pi by eight and similarly for the last
reduce so two brackets turn into one minus
chivari rendu cosines minus vasthai, so one minus brackets avthai
the reductions give negative cosines

steps.why: Two brackets with a plus and two with a minus is exactly the shape a difference of squares needs. The reduction is what creates it.
common_mistakes: Missing the minus and leaving all four as sums.

steps.label: Pair into differences of squares
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Pair each (1 + x) with its matching (1 − x). Each pair gives 1 − x², and 1 − cos² is sin².
steps.memory_tip: Pair each (1 + x) with its matching (1 − x): each pair gives 1 − x², and 1 − cos² is sin².

lines.text: Pair (1 + c)(1 − c) = 1 − c² for each angle:

recall.must_convey: That the brackets are paired into (1 − cos²) forms, which become sin².
accept: pair each plus bracket with its minus partner to get one minus cos squared which is sin squared
the pairs give differences of squares equal to sine squared
each pair becomes sin squared
prathi pair one minus cos square avthundi, ante sin square
pair them up into differences of squares

steps.why: Pairing the RIGHT brackets matters — pairing π/8 with 3π/8 would give nothing. Each bracket must meet its own negative.
common_mistakes: Pairing the brackets in the order written.

steps.label: Reduce sin(3π/8)
steps.margin_note: Third mark. sin(3π/8) is cos(π/8), so the product becomes sin² times cos² of the SAME angle — which the double-angle formula can handle.
steps.memory_tip: sin(3π/8) = cos(π/8), so the product is sin² times cos² of the SAME angle.

recall.must_convey: That sin(3π/8) = cos(π/8), so the product is sin²(π/8) cos²(π/8) in one angle.
accept: sin three pi by eight is cos pi by eight so both are in the same angle
reduce so the product is sin squared times cos squared of pi by eight
the second sine becomes a cosine of the same angle
sin three pi by eight ante cos pi by eight, so okate angle
both terms end up in pi by eight

steps.why: A product of a sine and cosine of the SAME angle can be written as a double angle. Getting both into one angle is what makes the last step possible.
common_mistakes: Leaving the two different angles and being unable to finish.

steps.label: Use the double angle
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Introduce a 1/4 so that 2 sin cos can be formed, then sin(π/4) = 1/√2.
steps.memory_tip: Introduce a 1/4 so 2 sin cos can be formed, then sin(π/4) = 1/√2.

lines.text: Make 2 sin θ cos θ appear: multiply inside the

recall.must_convey: That sin²cos² is written as (1/4)(2 sin cos)² = (1/4)sin²(π/4) = 1/8.
accept: write it as a quarter of two sin cos all squared which is a quarter of a half equal to one eighth
introduce the quarter so the double angle appears, giving one eighth
the answer is one over eight
quarter techi two sin cos square ga rasthe one eighth vasthundi
a quarter times a half is an eighth

steps.why: The 1/4 is manufactured on purpose so that the 2 sin cos pattern can appear. Nothing forces it — it is a choice that makes the last line work.
common_mistakes: Not introducing the 1/4 and being unable to form the double angle.

insider_note: Reduce the last two angles so they pair as (1 + x)(1 − x) with the first two. That leaves sin²·sin², and sin(3π/8) = cos(π/8) turns it into the double-angle form.
